chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Momentum and Trend Following Actually Are

lessons.title: Why Momentum Works: Behavioral Biases and Structural Explanations

children.text: Jegadeesh and Titman published their momentum finding in 1993. Every hedge fund, prop desk, and quant researcher on earth has had free access to it for more than three decades. In an efficient market, a publicly known, well documented source of excess return should get traded away almost immediately, as smart money rushes in to exploit it until the edge disappears. That is exactly what happened to most simple, mechanical anomalies discovered in finance research. It is not what happened to momentum. It has kept showing up, across dozens of countries and asset classes, for thirty years after publication. Understanding why requires looking at both how investors actually behave, not how theory assumes they behave, and at real structural frictions that keep the trade from being fully arbitraged away.

body.text: Momentum persists because prices adjust to new information gradually rather than instantly. Behavioral biases slow individual investors down, structural frictions slow institutions down, and the combination produces a drift that a disciplined trader can systematically capture, even though everyone involved knows the pattern exists.

children.text: Behavioral Explanation 1: Investors Underreact to News

markDefs.definition: The tendency to rely too heavily on an existing belief or prior price level, and to adjust that belief too slowly when new evidence arrives.

children.text: causes investors to hold onto their prior view of a company's value even after genuinely new, positive information arrives. When a company beats earnings estimates by a wide margin, investors do not instantly re-price the stock to reflect the full new picture. They revise their expectations partially, watch for confirmation, and revise further only as more evidence accumulates, a quarterly result, a management commentary, a follow-up brokerage note. Each partial revision shows up as further price movement in the same direction. The stock does not jump to its new fair value in one move, it drifts toward it over weeks or months, which is exactly the pattern a momentum strategy is built to capture.
Behavioral Explanation 2: Herding and the Bandwagon Effect

Once a trend is visibly underway, it attracts attention on its own terms, independent of new fundamental news. A stock making repeated new highs shows up on more screeners, more broker recommendation lists, and more retail trading app watchlists. Financial media coverage tends to follow price action rather than lead it, which means a stock that has already moved gets more headlines, which draws in more buyers, who push the trend further. This is herding: investors following the crowd rather than independently evaluating the asset. It is not irrational for any single investor to notice a strong trend and want to participate, but the collective effect is to extend a trend beyond what pure fundamentals alone would justify, at least for a while.

markDefs.definition: The well documented tendency of investors to sell winning positions too early, to lock in a gain, while holding losing positions too long, hoping to avoid realizing a loss.

children.text: , first documented by Shefrin and Statman in 1985, describes investors who sell winners too early to lock in a gain, and hold losers too long, unwilling to realize a loss. This creates a persistent, artificial source of selling pressure on a stock that has started to rise, since some holders exit early purely to bank the profit, not because their view of the company has changed. That early, non-informational selling caps how fast the price can move to reflect genuinely good news, spreading the price adjustment out over a longer period instead of one sharp jump, and reinforcing the same gradual-drift pattern anchoring produces.

body.text: Notice all three behavioral explanations point the same direction: they slow down how fast a price reaches its new fair value after genuine news. Momentum is not really a bet that prices will keep rising forever. It is a bet that the market's reaction to real information is spread out over months rather than compressed into a single instant.

children.text: Structural Explanation 1: Gradual Information Diffusion Through Institutions

A large mutual fund or FII that decides to build a meaningful position in an NSE-listed stock cannot simply place one order for the full size. Doing so would move the price sharply against itself, since the order itself is often larger than a normal day's liquidity in that stock. Institutional desks instead build positions gradually over days or weeks, sometimes visible afterward as bulk or block deals reported on the NSE and BSE. This buying pressure, spread out mechanically over time rather than concentrated on the day new information arrives, is itself a structural source of price drift that has nothing to do with any individual investor's psychology.

Sell-side analysts do not revise their earnings estimates and target prices in one step after a strong result. They typically update in stages, an initial reaction note on result day, a more detailed revision after the management earnings call, and further changes after a plant visit or a follow-up channel check. Each revision round can prompt a fresh wave of buying from investors who track analyst target price changes. This effect is often stronger, not weaker, outside the most heavily tracked large caps, since a midcap or smallcap stock followed by only two or three brokerages takes longer for its full information picture to become common knowledge than a Nifty 50 stock followed by thirty analysts.
Structural Explanation 3: Passive Flows and Index Inclusion

A stock that has been rising and gaining market capitalization becomes a candidate for inclusion in a major index like the Nifty 50 or Nifty 200. Once inclusion becomes likely, active fund managers often buy ahead of the change, anticipating the mechanical buying that will come from index funds and ETFs once the change is confirmed. That anticipatory buying itself adds further upward pressure, reinforcing the trend that made the stock a candidate for inclusion in the first place, well before any passive fund is forced to buy a single share.

children.text: Why Arbitrageurs Don't Simply Erase the Effect

markDefs.definition: The real-world frictions, costs, and risks that prevent sophisticated traders from fully eliminating a known market inefficiency simply by trading against it.

children.text: If momentum is this well known, why don't hedge funds simply trade it until the excess return vanishes? The honest answer sits under a broader idea called

. First, momentum strategies carry real crash risk, sharp, sudden reversals that can wipe out months of gains in days, which deters some capital from pursuing the strategy at full size. Second, fund managers are usually judged against a benchmark over short horizons, and a strategy that occasionally suffers a bad quarter, even if profitable over years, carries real career risk that keeps some capital on the sidelines. Third, shorting the weakest, lowest-momentum stocks in India is not frictionless: only stocks on SEBI's F&O eligible list have listed derivatives, and shorting anything outside that list through the securities lending and borrowing mechanism carries extra cost and operational complexity, which limits how fully the losing side of a momentum trade can be exploited by arbitrageurs. None of these frictions make momentum riskless. They explain why a known, published effect can still survive in a market full of professionals trying to exploit every edge they can find.

body.text: The same crash risk that keeps arbitrageurs from fully erasing momentum is a real risk for anyone trading it too. A strategy that has worked for thirty years in aggregate data can still lose money badly in a specific quarter when a crowded trend unwinds fast. Risk management for exactly this situation is covered later in this course.

body.title: Spot the explanation
body.question: A stock beats earnings estimates sharply. On result day it rises only 5%. Over the following two months, as three separate brokerages raise their target prices in sequence after digesting the management call and a follow-up plant visit, the stock rises another 20%. Which explanation for momentum does this best illustrate?
options: Herding, because retail investors are copying each other
The disposition effect, because winners are being sold too early
Analyst coverage lag, because the full picture is being priced in stages as coverage catches up
Index inclusion flows, because passive funds are forced to buy
body.explanation: The staged price reaction, tracking staged analyst revisions rather than one instant full repricing, is a textbook example of analyst coverage lag slowing down how fast new information gets fully reflected in the price.

body.title: How long has this been public knowledge?
body.prompt: It is 2026. Jegadeesh and Titman published their original momentum study in 1993. Roughly how many years has momentum now been a publicly documented finding in academic finance?
body.explanation: 33 years of public documentation, replication across more than 40 countries, and continued persistence despite every professional investor having free access to the research, is exactly the puzzle this lesson set out to explain.

body.title: Why doesn't the fund just short it fully?
body.scenario: A quant fund identifies a small-cap NSE stock in the bottom decile of 6-month momentum, a stock its model says should be shorted as part of a long-short momentum portfolio. The stock has no listed futures or options contract.
body.prompt: What structural friction, covered in this lesson, makes this short position harder to execute than shorting a Nifty 50 stock would be?
body.modelAnswer: Only stocks on SEBI's F&O eligible list have listed derivatives that make shorting simple and liquid. A stock without listed derivatives can only be shorted through the securities lending and borrowing mechanism, which carries extra cost, limited stock availability, and more operational complexity. This is a concrete example of a limit to arbitrage: the fund's model may be correct that the stock is a momentum loser, but the friction of actually executing the short reduces how fully that view can be expressed, which is part of why the momentum effect is not fully arbitraged away even by sophisticated funds.

points: Momentum persists because prices adjust to new information gradually, not instantly, which is what a momentum strategy is structurally built to capture.

Three behavioral biases slow down individual price adjustment: anchoring causes underreaction to news, herding extends visible trends, and the disposition effect spreads out selling pressure on winners.
Three structural frictions add to this: gradual institutional order execution, staged analyst coverage revisions, and anticipatory buying ahead of index inclusion.

Momentum survives despite being public for over 30 years because of limits to arbitrage: crash risk, career risk for fund managers, and real shorting frictions in markets like India's, where only F&O eligible stocks are easily shortable.
The same crash risk that limits arbitrage against momentum is a real risk for anyone trading it, a theme this course returns to when covering risk management.
